steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for our paper arguing that depression-prediction models do badly partly because of annotation quality, using the PRIMATE dataset as a case study. Cover how social media depression datasets are usually built and annotated, the move to symptom-level annotation, why we chose PRIMATE, and what our re-annotation shows.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Depression estimation from social media and how data is annotated
2. Existing depression datasets: sources and annotation methods
3. Fine-grained symptom annotation: D2S and PRIMATE
4. Our study: MHP re-annotation of PRIMATE for anhedonia

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Background
- NLP for estimating depression level from social media texts: widely researched in NLP for mental health
- posts from Twitter, Reddit
- annotated by crowd workers with brief training from a mental health professional (MHP) or only annotation instructions

2. Existing datasets
- mostly binary annotation (depressed or not)
- sources: Reddit; X (former Twitter)
- mostly automatic annotation: regex matching of self-reported terms ("I have been diagnosed with depression")
- some manual verification: layman crowd workers, or the authors themselves

3. Fine-grained annotation
- D2S (X) and PRIMATE (Reddit): depressed posts annotated with PHQ-9 symptoms
- both: crowd workers, later verified by MHPs, but different verification
- D2S: majority voting for conflicts, psychiatrist resolves ties; then 100 random samples for quality control verified by a psychiatrist
- another work: random sample of D2S annotated with explanations per symptom with two MHPs -> higher validity
- PRIMATE: no info on quality control -> validity concerns -> chosen for case study

4. Our study
- validity of mental health annotations by layman crowd workers is a concern
- our MHP (second author, practising clinical psychology intern) reannotated 170 PRIMATE posts for lack of interest or pleasure (anhedonia)
- finer labels: "mentioned" vs "answerable", extra "writer's symptom" label; evidence spans
- many false positives in PRIMATE labels; related to difficulty of conceptualizing anhedonia
- release under Data Use Agreement (DUA); higher-quality test set for anhedonia detection

steps.text:
Using various NLP techniques to automatically estimate the level of depression from social media texts is a widely researched topic in NLP applied to mental health. Most of these datasets are made of online posts collected from popular social media platforms like Twitter or Reddit. The posts are usually annotated by crowd workers who only had a short training with a mental health professional (MHP), or who sometimes only had the annotation instructions.

There are multiple depression-related datasets based on social media texts, but most of them only have binary annotation, i.e. whether the user is depressed or not. The most common data sources are Reddit and X (former Twitter). Most of the studies annotate with automatic methods, such as matching self-reported terms with regular expressions, like "I have been diagnosed with depression". Some of them do manual verification and annotation, either with layman crowd workers or by the authors themselves.

[Fine-grained annotation]
- recent interest; D2S (X) and PRIMATE (Reddit), PHQ-9 symptoms
- crowd workers + MHP verification, but process differs
- D2S: majority voting, psychiatrist resolves ties, 100 random samples checked by psychiatrist; another work added explanations per symptom with two MHPs
- PRIMATE: no info on quality control -> concern -> our case study

[Our study]
- MHP (second author, clinical psychology intern) reannotated 170 posts for anhedonia
- "mentioned" vs "answerable", "writer's symptom", evidence spans
- many false positives; conceptualizing anhedonia is hard
- DUA release, higher-quality test set

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Using various NLP techniques to automatically estimate the level of depression from social media texts is a widely researched topic in NLP applied to mental health. Most of these datasets are made of online posts collected from popular social media platforms like Twitter or Reddit. The posts are usually annotated by crowd workers who only had a short training with a mental health professional (MHP), or who sometimes only had the annotation instructions.

There are multiple depression-related datasets based on social media texts, but most of them only have binary annotation, i.e. whether the user is depressed or not. The most common data sources are Reddit and X (former Twitter). Most of the studies annotate with automatic methods, such as matching self-reported terms with regular expressions, like "I have been diagnosed with depression". Some of them do manual verification and annotation, either with layman crowd workers or by the authors themselves.

Recently there has been interest in more fine-grained annotation of depression. In particular, two recent datasets, D2S and PRIMATE, identify depressed social media posts from X and Reddit, respectively, and annotate them with PHQ-9 symptoms. Both datasets were annotated with the help of crowd workers and then verified by MHPs. But the verification process was not the same. For D2S, conflicting annotations were resolved by majority voting, and the psychiatrist resolved the ties. After that, 100 random samples were selected for quality control and a psychiatrist verified them. Additionally, other work annotated a random sample of D2S with explanations for each symptom with the help of two MHPs, which increases the validity of the data. For PRIMATE, there is no information given about the quality control procedure. This raises concerns about whether the annotations are valid, so we selected PRIMATE for our case study.

In this study, we use the PRIMATE dataset as an example to show that the validity of annotations for mental health data is a concern when they are done by layman crowd workers. Our MHP reannotated 170 posts from the PRIMATE dataset for the symptom of lack of interest or pleasure (anhedonia). The MHP is the second author of the paper, and is also a practising clinical psychology intern. Our annotations have more fine-grained labels ("mentioned" vs "answerable", and also an additional "writer's symptom" label), and also spans of text that serve as evidence for the labels. We see a high number of false positives in the PRIMATE labels, which may be related to how hard it is to conceptualize anhedonia. The annotations will be released under a Data Use Agreement (DUA), and we believe they can serve as a higher-quality test set for detecting anhedonia.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Applying various NLP techniques to automatically estimate the depression level from social media texts has been a widely researched topic in the field of NLP applied to mental health. Most of these datasets consist of online posts gathered from popular social media platforms such as Twitter or Reddit. These posts are usually annotated by crowd workers who had only brief training with a mental health professional (MHP) or sometimes only had access to the annotation instructions.

While multiple depression-related datasets based on social media texts exist, most of them only present binary annotation, i.e. whether the user is depressed or not. The most common sources of data are Reddit [1,2,3] and X (former Twitter) [4,5]. Most studies use automatic annotation methods, such as regular expression matching of self-reported terms like "I have been diagnosed with depression". Some of them perform manual verification and annotation, either via layman crowd workers [2] or by the authors themselves [4,1].

Recently, interest in more fine-grained depression annotation has emerged. In particular, two recent datasets, D2S [6] and PRIMATE [7], identify depressed social media posts from X and Reddit, respectively, and annotate them with PHQ-9 symptoms [8]. Both datasets were annotated with the help of crowd workers and later verified by MHPs. However, the verification process differed. For D2S, conflicting annotations were resolved by majority voting, and the psychiatrist resolved the ties. After that, 100 random samples were selected for quality control and verified by a psychiatrist. Additionally, [9] annotated a random sample of D2S with explanations for each symptom with the help of two MHPs, increasing the validity of the data. In the case of PRIMATE, no information is given on the quality control procedure. This raises concerns about the validity of the annotations; thus, we selected PRIMATE for our case study.

In this study, using the PRIMATE dataset as an example, we show that the validity of annotations for mental health data is a concern when they are performed by layman crowd workers. Our MHP reannotated 170 posts from the PRIMATE dataset for the lack of interest or pleasure (anhedonia) symptom. The MHP is the second author of the paper and a practising clinical psychology intern. Our annotations include more fine-grained labels ("mentioned" vs "answerable", as well as an additional "writer's symptom" label) as well as text spans that serve as evidence for the labels. We observe a high number of false positives in the PRIMATE labels, which can be related to the high difficulty of conceptualizing anhedonia [10]. The annotations will be released under a Data Use Agreement (DUA), and we believe they can serve as a higher-quality test set for anhedonia detection.
